title: The Decarbonisation of European Ports
summary: European ports face a mandatory transformation, driven by an aggressive suite of EU legislation like FuelEU Maritime and the expanded EU ETS, not genuine voluntary greening initiatives. This regulatory onslaught directly targets shipping lines and fuel suppliers, imposing strict compliance and significant financial penalties for failing to reduce emissions. dirtiestships.com will be watching closely to see if these mandated infrastructure changes deliver actual carbon intensity reductions or merely create new avenues for greenwashing and compliance reporting.
content:
European ports are being remade. Long established as cargo-handling facilities, they are becoming multi-functional nodes at the intersection of the energy transition, digitalisation and infrastructure resilience: gateways for conventional trade, industrial platforms for renewable energy and sustainable fuels, receiving terminals for hydrogen, ammonia and captured CO2, and marshalling hubs for offshore wind.

The transformation is not voluntary. It is driven by a prescriptive body of EU legislation spanning climate, transport, energy, competition, security, waste and industrial policy, binding on port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, fuel suppliers, service providers and Member States. The principal instruments are the FuelEU Maritime Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805), the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1804), the extension of the EU Emissions Trading System to maritime transport (Directive 2003/87/EC as amended by Directive (EU) 2023/959), the revised TEN-T Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1679), the reformed State aid framework, the NIS2 and Critical Entities Resilience Directives, the Seveso III Directive, the Port Reception Facilities Directive and the EU Taxonomy.

Two developments external to that framework now condition everything within it.

The first is the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework. Approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, its adoption was adjourned at an extraordinary session in October 2025 by 57 votes to 49, and the session reconvenes in the autumn of 2026. Whether a global fuel intensity standard and carbon pricing mechanism is adopted, and in what form, determines whether the EU’s regional measures remain the operative constraint on shipping calling at European ports or become one layer of a two-tier system. The July 2026 EU ETS review proposal expressly anticipates the question.

The second is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the outbreak of hostilities in the Gulf on 28 February 2026. Roughly a fifth of seaborne LNG and a third of seaborne crude normally transits the strait, and Europe draws 12% to 14% of its LNG from Qatar through it. Brent moved from below $60 at the start of 2026 to above $100, European gas prices rose by between 40% and 67%, and the Commission’s spring 2026 forecast revised its Brent assumption upwards by 46%. The consequences run through this analysis: the economics of LNG import terminals, the price assumptions underlying power purchase agreements, the political appetite for energy sovereignty investment, and the State aid framework itself, amended in April 2026 to accommodate the shock. They also explain why the EU Ports Strategy of March 2026 gives as much weight to security, dual-use capability and foreign ownership as to decarbonisation.

This article examines the progress European ports have made, the regulatory and commercial challenges they face, and how contractual, institutional and financing structures are adapting. Its focus is maritime ports; the Ports Strategy covers inland ports too, and much of the funding and permitting analysis applies to them, but their traffic profile and regulatory position warrant separate treatment.

2.The decarbonisation imperative:

Principal challenges

2.1Grid capacity, and the law that governs it

Electrification — on-shore power supply (“OPS”) for vessels at berth, electric cranes and automated guided vehicles, and port-side renewable generation — places extraordinary demands on local electrical infrastructure. Existing capacity is frequently insufficient. The AFIR obligation to provide OPS by 2030 requires in many cases new high-voltage connections, substations and distribution networks, with lead times often exceeding five years, against a background of congested distribution grids and connection backlogs stretching years into the future.

Ports have responded by building dedicated on-site generation — solar arrays, port-side turbines and battery storage — creating behind-the-meter microgrids capable of meeting a substantial share of demand independently of the national grid.

The legal framework governing that strategy is examined less often than the engineering, and it is where the difficulties lie. A port that generates electricity and supplies it to terminal operators, tenants and visiting vessels is carrying on a supply activity subject to national licensing. The principal enabling structure is Article 38 of Directive (EU) 2019/944, under which a national regulatory authority may classify a network distributing electricity within a geographically confined industrial or commercial site as a closed distribution system, exempting the operator from certain tariff approval and third-party access obligations. Whether a port qualifies, and on what conditions, is a matter of national implementation and varies considerably.

Where the status is unavailable, the port must hold a supply licence, contract through a licensed supplier, or structure the arrangement as private wire or direct-line supply — each with different tariff, metering and network charge consequences.

Two points bear on the timetable. Non-firm or flexible connection agreements, under which connection is granted earlier in exchange for curtailment during system stress, are now the principal practical route to accelerating access, and may be entirely adequate for a port whose peak demand is driven by intermittent vessel connection events and which holds battery storage.

And the cost allocation rules for deep reinforcement differ markedly between Member States, determining whether the port or the network operator bears

the cost of upstream works its connection triggers. Both should be resolved before the OPS investment decision, not after.

2.2Fuel technology uncertainty

The sector has not converged on a dominant alternative fuel. Green hydrogen, ammonia, e-methanol, bio-LNG and synthetic e-fuels each present distinct advantages in energy density, safety profile, cost, scalability and compatibility with existing propulsion.

Operators therefore face a material technology risk: capital committed to infrastructure for a fuel that may not reach commercial scale, or may be superseded before the investment is recovered. The risk is acute for smaller ports that cannot hedge across multiple pathways.

2.3Scope 3 emissions and the limits of port authority control

Port authorities control their own operational emissions and those attributable to purchased energy, but the overwhelming majority of a port’s footprint derives from calling vessels and from the landside chains serving it. A further component comprises emissions from service providers operating within the port area — bunker suppliers, storage terminal operators, waste reception providers, ship repair facilities — whose activities form part of the value chain but fall outside the authority’s control. This asymmetry between accountability and control is among the most intractable problems in port decarbonisation and drives the contractual innovation discussed in Section 10.

One qualification is now necessary. Much of that contractual cascade assumed port authorities would themselves be subject to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and would need granular Scope 3 data from tenants to comply.

The Omnibus simplification package and the accompanying “stop the clock” measures have narrowed CSRD scope and deferred its application, so a significant number of port authorities may no longer be in scope, or only from a later date. The commercial drivers for data collection remain, and cargo owners subject to their own reporting obligations continue to demand it. But drafters should not assume a statutory obligation that may no longer apply to their client, and should consider anchoring data provisions in the counterparty’s requirements rather than the port’s.

2.4Techniques being deployed

OPS, or cold ironing, allows vessels to shut down auxiliary engines at berth and draw power from shore. On-site generation coupled with battery storage is creating port-level microgrids operating with a degree of independence from the national grid.

Bilbao is deploying approximately 50 MW of local renewable capacity to feed its 30 MW BilbOPS network, aiming to generate at least a quarter of its ship-power demand on site. Valencia, constrained by dense urban surroundings and limited grid headroom, is executing the EU-backed RENEWPORT project, installing a vertical photovoltaic wall onto the breakwater of its northern expansion and converting wave-protection infrastructure into a generation asset.

Rotterdam has installed multi-megawatt turbines on its outer seawalls at the Maasvlakte, paired with battery storage to buffer intermittent output and absorb the load spikes that occur when large container vessels connect. Antwerp-Bruges operates on-site turbines managed through an internal smart grid, powering automated terminal vehicles and electric straddle carriers.

Several major ports are additionally building electrolyser capacity with associated storage and pipeline infrastructure. Terminal operators are replacing diesel yard equipment with electric rubber-tyred gantry cranes, automated stacking cranes and battery-electric AGVs integrated with energy-optimising terminal operating systems.

Where full electrification is not yet feasible, ports are turning to drop-in biofuels, whose supply constraints are examined at Section 4.3.

3.The EU regulatory framework:

Key instruments and their impact

3.1The FuelEU Maritime Regulation

The FuelEU Maritime Regulation (“FuelEU”) imposes progressively stringent limits on the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by ships calling at EU ports, measured well-to-wake. The trajectory begins at 2% from 1 January 2025 and escalates to 6% by 2030,

14.5% by 2035, 31% by 2040, 62% by 2045 and 80% by 2050. From 2030, container and passenger vessels at berth in core TEN-T ports must connect to OPS or use equivalent zero-emission technology.

Four features of the compliance mechanism are commercially material and frequently overlooked.

First, energy from renewable fuels of non-biological origin (“RFNBOs”) attracts a multiplier of two in the intensity calculation until the end of 2033, materially improving the compliance value of green hydrogen and its derivatives relative to biofuels. From 2034 a 2% RFNBO sub-quota applies if the RFNBO share has not reached 1% by 2031. For ports investing in electrolysis, the multiplier is the near-term demand driver and the sub-quota the medium-term one.

Second, compliance is not strictly vessel-by-vessel. FuelEU permits pooling of compliance balances between ships, banking of surpluses and limited borrowing against future periods. A market in surpluses has developed, and the price at which they trade directly determines a line’s willingness to pay a premium for compliant fuel at a given port.

Third, the penalty for non-compliance is calculated at a rate equivalent to €2,400 per tonne of VLSFO-equivalent energy. That figure is an effective ceiling on the green premium a supplier can command: no owner pays more for compliant fuel than the penalty it avoids.

Fourth, persistent non-compliance carries an access consequence. Where a ship has failed to comply for two or more consecutive reporting periods and other enforcement has not secured compliance, the Member State of the port of call may issue an expulsion order refusing the ship entry to EU ports. Berth booking terms and terminal use agreements should accommodate the possibility that a vessel with a confirmed booking becomes ineligible to call.

For ports the consequence is twofold: they must ensure compliant fuels are available in sufficient quantity and at competitive prices to attract calls, and must invest in the OPS infrastructure the berth-side requirement demands. The corridor model discussed at Section 12 offers one route to the committed offtake necessary to justify that investment.

3.2The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation

The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (“AFIR”) imposes deployment obligations on Member States. The OPS obligation is commonly described as applying to all core TEN-T ports. It does not. Under Article 9 it is triggered by traffic thresholds averaged over the preceding three years: at least 100 calls of container ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, 40 calls of ro-ro passenger ships and high-speed craft above that tonnage, or 25 calls of other passenger ships. Where a threshold is met, the Member State must ensure supply sufficient for at least 90% of qualifying calls by 1 January 2030. Exemptions apply where the port is not grid-connected, where connection cost would be disproportionate to benefit, or where demand is insufficient.

The distinction matters. A port below the thresholds has no AFIR obligation but may still face commercial pressure from vessels subject to the FuelEU berth-side requirement, which is drafted by reference to core TEN-T status rather than to AFIR thresholds.

The two instruments are not perfectly aligned, and the gap between them is a live question for mid-tier ports.

The LNG obligation is similarly qualified: an appropriate number of core TEN-T ports must provide bunkering, not all of them. Hydrogen refuelling is encouraged, not mandated. AFIR has nonetheless triggered an urgent programme of electrical upgrades, with ports competing for grid capacity, transformer equipment and specialist engineering resource in short supply.

3.3The EU Ports Strategy (2026)

On 4 March 2026 the Commission adopted the EU Ports Strategy (COM(2026) 112 final), alongside a companion EU Industrial Maritime Strategy on shipbuilding and shipping. The Council adopted Conclusions in June 2026.

The Ports Strategy is a Commission Communication. It has no binding force of itself, and its objectives require implementation through subsequent legislation before they generate enforceable obligations — a point developed at Section 3.4, because it is easily and consequentially misapplied.

Its significance lies in what it signals, and in how much of it is not about decarbonisation:

•Competitiveness, innovation and digitalisation, including support for moving European port innovation beyond the pilot phase.

•Energy transition and clean industry, covering electrification, grid access, clean fuels, port-centred energy cooperation and faster permitting for strategic projects, with onshore power supply prioritised in a 2026 Connecting Europe Facility call.

•Protection and security, identifying ports as vulnerable to organised crime and drug trafficking, cyberattack and hybrid threats, with updated security guidance, a background-check framework for port workers and assessments of third-country ports.

•Economic security and foreign control, under which the Commission will develop criteria on foreign ownership and control of ports identified as strategic dual-use infrastructure, and on EU investment in third-country ports.

•Resilience and preparedness, including military mobility, port climate resilience planning, and a capacity-building programme for small and medium ports delivered with EIB Advisory.

The security, foreign ownership and dual-use strands are likely to generate as much advisory work over the next three years as the energy transition strand, and interact with the foreign investment conditions proposed in the Industrial Accelerator Act.

3.4Permitting acceleration: what is actually binding

The Ports Strategy identifies protracted permitting as a principal impediment to green infrastructure. It cannot itself do anything about that. Nor, contrary to a widespread misapprehension, can the Clean Industrial Deal, which is likewise a Commission Communication, adopted on 26 February 2025, prescribing no permitting deadlines of any kind.

Three instruments are relevant; only two are law.

RED III. The Renewable Energy Directive (Directive (EU) 2023/2413) (“RED III”) contains the permitting regime that is already binding, already transposed and most directly applicable to port renewable projects. It requires Member States to designate renewables acceleration areas and imposes maximum permit-granting deadlines: broadly twelve months within designated areas and twenty-four months outside them, with shorter periods for solar and for repowering. Article 16f establishes a presumption that renewable plants, their grid connection and associated storage are in the overriding public interest and serve public health and safety, for the purposes of the derogations available under the Habitats and Birds Directives and the Water Framework Directive. For a port

constructing solar arrays, port-side turbines, battery storage or the grid connection serving them, this is the first place to look, and its omission from most port decarbonisation commentary is hard to explain.

The NZIA. The Net-Zero Industry Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1735) (“NZIA”) establishes streamlined permitting for the manufacturing of net-zero technologies — electrolysers and fuel cells, batteries and storage, heat pumps, and renewable energy equipment including solar and wind components.

Qualifying projects benefit from a single national competent authority acting as one-stop shop and from binding maximum timeframes: twelve months below one gigawatt of annual manufacturing capacity and eighteen months at or above it, reduced to nine and twelve months for recognised net-zero strategic projects, with a deemed grant of consent where the authority fails to decide in time.

The Decarbonisation of European Ports • 7

Its limitation is material scope. The NZIA applies to manufacturing, not to deployment or installation as end-use infrastructure. An OPS network, an ammonia bunkering facility, a hydrogen refuelling installation or a shore-side storage terminal is deployment and falls outside it. Where the NZIA genuinely assists ports is port-based manufacturing, of which floating offshore wind foundation fabrication is the clearest example: the scale of the structures requires fabrication, integration and float-out from deep-water facilities with reinforced quaysides and heavy-lift capacity, and the Commission’s State aid clearances for such facilities (Section 5.3) confirm that the EU institutions treat them as clean energy industrial activity. If manufacturing floating foundations constitutes production of renewable energy equipment, the facility should qualify and attract the NZIA timeframes.

The Industrial Accelerator Act. On 4 March 2026, the same day as the Ports Strategy, the Commission published its proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act (COM(2026) 100 final) (“IAA”). It would extend NZIA-style permitting — a single digital point of contact, maximum timelines, tacit approval at intermediate stages — to energy-intensive decarbonisation projects generally, require each Member State to designate at least one Industrial Manufacturing Acceleration Area with area-wide baseline permits within twelve months of entry into force, introduce minimum low-carbon and Union-origin content requirements in public procurement and support schemes from 1 January 2029, and impose conditions on foreign direct investment above €100 million in strategic sectors.

The IAA is a proposal, in first reading under a joint committee procedure. Its permitting articles would apply one year after entry into force, and entry into force is not expected before 2027. It is something to plan around, not to rely on. Advice predicated on the availability of Clean Industrial Deal permitting acceleration for a project reaching financial close in 2026 or 2027 is predicated on an instrument that does not exist.

8 • The Decarbonisation of European Ports

The position today is therefore: RED III for renewable generation, storage and associated connection; the NZIA for genuine on-site manufacturing; and for everything else — OPS, bunkering, fuel storage, hydrogen distribution — the ordinary national process, with the Seveso III, environmental impact assessment, habitats and water requirements discussed at Section 11.4 applying in full.

3.5The IMO Net-Zero Framework and its interaction with EU measures

The EU’s regional measures were enacted in the expectation that a global measure would follow. Whether it does is now the largest open question in maritime decarbonisation, and it bears directly on the investment case for European port infrastructure.

The Net-Zero Framework, approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, would introduce into a new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI a global greenhouse gas fuel intensity standard for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, coupled with a pricing and reward mechanism: ships exceeding the thresholds acquire remedial units at set prices, ships using zero or near-zero emission fuels earn surplus units and rewards, and revenues are channelled through an IMO Net-Zero Fund. Adoption was scheduled for an extraordinary session of the MEPC in October 2025. After an unusually political session, a motion to adjourn for one year carried by 57 votes to 49 with 21 abstentions. The designation of the North-East Atlantic as an Emission Control Area for SOx, particulate matter and NOx — of direct consequence for northern European ports — fell with it.

Technical work on the implementation guidelines has continued, and the session reconvenes in the autumn of 2026. If the Framework is adopted then, tacit acceptance would put entry into force approximately sixteen months later, with a first reporting year around 2028. It is equally possible that the text is materially modified before it reaches the floor, or that adoption fails again.

Three consequences follow.

Double payment. A ship on a voyage into an EU port would, if both regimes operate, face an ETS surrender obligation, a FuelEU compliance obligation and an IMO remedial unit obligation for the same emissions. The July 2026 ETS review proposal introduces a review clause to address this, and FuelEU contains its own review provision. Neither says what the adjustment would be. The possibilities range from full EU alignment with the global measure, through credit for IMO remedial units against ETS obligations, to retention of both regimes with narrowed EU scope. ESPO’s stated preference is a global agreement followed promptly by EU alignment.

Carbon leakage. Much of the competitive disadvantage EU ports complain of arises from the regional character of the EU measures. A global instrument would remove a substantial part of the incentive to route cargo through non-EU hubs and would correspondingly reduce the urgency of the anti-evasion measures at Section 5.1.

Contractual drafting. Long-term fuel supply agreements, terminal use agreements, charterparties and finance documents negotiated now will be performed across the period in which this resolves. Regulatory change provisions should be drafted by reference to the specific possibility of a global measure entering into force and of consequential EU amendment, rather than to generic change-in-law language. Where a project’s revenue model depends on the green premium European regulation currently supports, the sensitivity of that premium to EU alignment should be modelled explicitly.

4.Sectoral adaptation: How port and terminal operators are responding

4.1Container and passenger terminals

Container and passenger operators are at the forefront of AFIR and FuelEU compliance. The energy demands of large container vessels and cruise ships at berth are substantial, and the 2030 obligation has required major investment in high-voltage shore connections, often with dedicated grid reinforcement. Cruise terminals face particular difficulty given very high vessel power consumption and the proximity of many berths to urban centres where capacity is already constrained. Operators are entering long-term partnerships with utilities and grid operators, and exploring green bonds and public-private structures to fund the work. The urban location of many cruise berths also brings the recast Ambient Air Quality Directive into play, as Section 11.4 explains.

4.2Liquid bulk and LNG terminals

Operators here must future-proof existing infrastructure against declining fossil throughput while positioning for growth in alternative commodities. Leading operators are designing tankage, pipeline systems and loading arms flexible enough to handle ammonia, liquefied hydrogen, e-methanol and bio-LNG alongside conventional hydrocarbons — additional capital expenditure that preserves optionality. Conversion of LNG import terminals to handle biomethane and synthetic methane is also proceeding, with the Świnoujście terminal in Poland pioneering the certification and integration of pipeline biomethane into existing infrastructure.

The effect of the Gulf disruption. The strategic calculus has been disturbed by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Qatari volumes, normally 12% to 14% of European LNG, have been curtailed and prices rose sharply through the first half of 2026. The immediate consequence is a reassertion of the security-of-supply case for import capacity that had, until early 2026, been increasingly hard to make against declining projected demand and Taxonomy exclusion.

Operators contemplating conversion or closure are weighing a materially different price and utilisation environment, and Member States are more receptive to public support for regasification than they were a year ago. Whether this is a durable shift or a cyclical interruption is unresolved; but capital allocation decisions taken during 2026 will be lived with for twenty years, and the divergence between short-term security imperatives and long-term Taxonomy alignment is now a boardroom question rather than a theoretical one.

The Methane Regulation. Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 operates on two planes. It imposes monitoring, reporting and verification obligations directly on operators of LNG import, regasification and storage terminals, requiring them to quantify and report emission sources, run leak detection and repair programmes, and comply with tightening limits on venting and flaring. More consequentially, it requires importers of fossil energy to demonstrate from 2030 that imported LNG meets maximum methane intensity values across the full upstream chain, with penalties and ultimately import restrictions for those who cannot. This is already reshaping terminal use agreements and LNG sale and purchase agreements: importers are incorporating methane intensity warranties and upstream disclosure obligations, while terminal operators are asked to provide enhanced segregation, metering and documentation for chain-of-custody verification. Biomethane and synthetic methane from non-fossil feedstocks fall outside the intensity requirements, adding a regulatory argument to the commercial case for conversion.

Bio-LNG chain of custody. A related difficulty arises where bio-LNG is produced from biomethane physically commingled with fossil gas in transport. Once injected into a grid, biomethane is chemically indistinguishable from fossil methane, and the gas withdrawn at the liquefaction facility is not in any physical sense the gas produced from renewable feedstocks. RED III addresses this by mass balancing supported by Guarantees of Origin: the producer registers the quantity and sustainability characteristics of gas injected, and a corresponding quantity withdrawn elsewhere may be designated renewable provided the Guarantee is transferred and cancelled through the applicable national registry.

Mass balancing allows biomethane to be traded across interconnected networks without dedicated pipelines, a practical necessity given European gas infrastructure. It introduces complexity at the point of liquefaction and supply as bunker fuel, because FuelEU requires verified lifecycle emissions data for each unit consumed, covering the full upstream chain. The Union Database for Biofuels, once fully operational with all Member States connected, is designed as a single electronic chain-of-custody platform tracking consignments from production through injection, mass balance transfer and withdrawal to final consumption, replacing the current fragmentation between national registries. For biomethane injected in one Member State and withdrawn for liquefaction in another, it should in principle supply the documentary chain FuelEU verification requires.

One residual difficulty persists. It is not settled whether fugitive methane emissions from the third-party network are attributed to the fuel’s lifecycle profile under the FuelEU well-to-wake methodology. If they are, the intensity advantage on which the preferential treatment of grid-transported biomethane depends may be materially eroded, and the interaction with the Methane Regulation’s own MRV framework becomes the operative question.

CBAM. Terminals handling imported ammonia should note that ammonia falls within the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Regulation (EU) 2023/956) (“CBAM”), whose definitive regime began on 1 January 2026. Importers must surrender certificates reflecting embedded emissions, net of any carbon price paid in the country of production. For ports positioning themselves as ammonia import hubs — Wilhelmshaven and Rotterdam prominent among them — the practical questions are who bears the CBAM cost and reporting burden as between terminal operator, importer of record and offtaker, and how the embedded emissions of ammonia produced from renewable hydrogen are evidenced. The interaction between CBAM verification and RFNBO certification under the delegated acts discussed at Section 5.4 is not fully worked through, and terminal use agreements should allocate the risk expressly rather than leaving it to a general tax and duties clause.

4.3Dry bulk terminals

Dry bulk operators are focusing on electrifying cargo-handling equipment: ship-to-shore cranes, conveyors, stackers, reclaimers and yard vehicles. Substituting electric for diesel plant is a relatively straightforward path to Scope 1 reductions, though capital costs are significant and the case is complicated by the long remaining life of existing equipment.

Where full electrification is not yet feasible — large wheel loaders, dump trucks, rail-mounted grab cranes with extended duty cycles — operators are adopting bio-diesel and hydrotreated vegetable oil (“HVO”) as drop-in replacements, enabling immediate reductions without wholesale fleet replacement. The strategy is particularly relevant in dry bulk, where duty cycles render battery-electric alternatives less mature than in container terminals. Operators here also face increasing pressure from charterers and cargo owners to demonstrate verifiable reductions, driving demand for digital monitoring.

Viability is materially constrained by competing demand from road haulage, which exerts dominant purchasing power. RED III establishes binding transport targets that Member States have implemented principally through blending mandates on road fuel suppliers, channelling available supply towards road diesel pools because those suppliers face penalties for missing incorporation requirements. Several Member States have reinforced the asymmetry through national measures — Germany’s Treibhausgasminderungsquote and the Netherlands’ renewable energy transport obligation among them — under which the compliance value of biofuels in the road pool exceeds the value obtainable for port-side use, creating a price premium that diverts supply. Terminal operators therefore face both price competition and physical availability risk, a constraint likely to intensify as RED III targets tighten through 2030. Security of supply should be assessed jurisdiction by jurisdiction, having regard to national blending mandates and to whether port-side consumption generates compliance credits on terms comparable to road transport.

5.EU ETS, TEN-T and State aid:

Impact on development and financing

5.1The EU ETS and maritime transport

Shipping companies operating vessels of 5,000 gross tonnage and above must surrender allowances for verified CO2 emissions on voyages within the EU and for 50% of emissions on voyages between EU and non-EU ports. The phase-in required surrender for 40% of verified emissions in 2024, 70% in 2025 and 100% from 2026.

The anti-evasion mechanism. The principal risk for EU ports is diversion of cargo to non-EU transhipment hubs in the United Kingdom, North Africa, Turkey or the Western Balkans. The mechanism already addressing this is frequently misdescribed. Article 3ga(2) provides that a stop by a container ship at a designated “neighbouring container transhipment port” is not treated as a port of call for determining the start or end of a voyage. Inserting such a stop therefore does not shorten the ETS-relevant leg: the longer voyage still counts. Tanger Med and East Port Said have been designated from the outset. The mechanism disregards the evasive call; it does not extend the ETS to the non-EU port.

Its limitation is narrowness. It applies only to container ships, only to ports meeting a 65% transhipment threshold, and only to a list reviewed biennially.

Commission analysis in March 2025 found no systemic evidence of evasive port calls, and traffic patterns comparing 2023 with 2024 were mixed rather than uniformly adverse. ESPO and FEPORT nonetheless maintain the risk is real and grows as scope reaches 100% of liable emissions in 2026.

The July 2026 review proposal. Published on 17 July 2026, its maritime elements go well beyond evasion:

•The list of neighbouring container transhipment ports would be reviewed annually rather than biennially, the 65% threshold reduced,

and criteria assessing a port’s capacity to accommodate transhipment traffic introduced.

•Scope would extend to ships between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage, with a commensurate cap increase, and to offshore operations.

•A Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion mechanism would recycle ETS revenues into sector decarbonisation, supported by a new allowance reserve for sustainable fuels and zero-emission propulsion.

•MRV and FuelEU reporting would be integrated and responsible entity definitions aligned.

•Ice-class and structural-constraint derogations would be extended to the end of 2035.

•A review clause would address double payment should global IMO measures enter into force.

Reception in the port sector has been qualified. FEPORT observes that the measures will not capture all avoidance, including relay traffic passing through an EU port where cargo origin and destination both lie outside the Union, and criticises the absence of targeted funding for port alternative fuel infrastructure. ESPO asks for the 65% criterion to be lifted rather than lowered, opposes broadening the vessel scope, seeks attention to outermost regions, and argues for a much larger share of maritime ETS revenue to return to port investment. The June 2026 Council Conclusions likewise called for corrective measures. The proposal remains subject to the ordinary legislative procedure.

Revenue recycling. A portion of ETS revenue is channelled through the Innovation Fund to support low-carbon deployment including port infrastructure, and ports are accessing grants to co-finance OPS, hydrogen production and storage. Within the framework discussed at Section 5.4, such grants function as catalytic instruments to unlock private capital rather than as standalone subsidies. The proposed SMAP mechanism would formalise and expand this.

5.2 The revised TEN-T guidelines and the Taxonomy filter

The revised TEN-T Regulation classifies infrastructure into Core, Extended Core and Comprehensive networks with differentiated priorities. Core classification confers priority access to Connecting Europe Facility funding and imposes binding requirements on multimodal connectivity, digitalisation and alternative fuel infrastructure.

Classification also operates as a funding gateway: a port outside the Core or Comprehensive network is in practice excluded from the principal EU pools for green maritime infrastructure. A second filter applies alongside it — alignment with the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852), under which fossil gas infrastructure is effectively excluded while hydrogen, ammonia, electrification and e-fuel projects benefit from presumptive eligibility. Funding is now explicitly conditioned on green benchmarks, so a port seeking co-financing for capacity expansion must demonstrate integration of rail connections, digital traffic management and alternative fuel bunkering into the design. This is reshaping project scope, compelling promoters to incorporate elements not commercially justified standing alone.

The Taxonomy’s gateway role makes reform of its technical screening criteria consequential. In early 2026 the Commission proposed amendments to the Climate and Environmental Delegated Acts simplifying the approximately 300 “do no significant harm” tests, which have been a material burden

for port promoters. The Platform on Sustainable Finance responded with 280 recommendations directed at preserving environmental integrity, including advocacy for mandatory lifecycle emission limits for maritime transport by January 2030 and concern that reduced CSRD granularity may deprive investors of verification data. Revised Delegated Acts are being finalised for entry into force on 1 January 2027. Until then the existing criteria apply, and structures predicated on the anticipated simplification carry the risk that the final criteria differ materially.

5.3State aid: the prior question, and the frameworks

Is it aid at all? Discussion tends to begin with the exemptions and skip the anterior question of whether the measure is aid within Article 107(1) TFEU. Following Leipzig-Halle, construction of infrastructure destined for commercial exploitation is an economic activity, and public funding of it may constitute aid to the operator. The Commission’s Notice on the Notion of State Aid addresses port infrastructure specifically, distinguishing general infrastructure serving the public at large, which is not aid, from infrastructure dedicated to economic exploitation, which may be. Navigation channels, breakwaters, locks and public roads within the port typically fall on the non-aid side; quay walls, terminals, warehousing and superstructure typically do not. The analysis must be conducted at three levels — aid to the port authority as owner, to the concessionaire, and to users — with an open, transparent, non-discriminatory and unconditional tender and market-rate charges being the principal means of excluding aid at the second and third.

The tax treatment of port authorities remains live. The Commission has required the Netherlands, France, Belgium, Italy and Spain to end corporate tax exemptions for their ports, and the principal challenges have been unsuccessful before the European courts. The tax position of the port authority is a starting point for any funding structure, because it affects both the aid analysis and the net cost of the investment.

GBER. Under the General Block Exemption Regulation (Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014, as amended) (the “GBER”), Member States are permitted to fund, without prior notification, port microgrids, OPS installations, hydrogen and ammonia refuelling infrastructure and other clean energy assets. For port investment specifically, Articles 56b and 56c are the operative provisions, covering maritime and inland ports respectively, with their own thresholds, eligible cost definitions and intensity ceilings calculated by reference to the funding gap — the difference between eligible costs and the net present value of expected revenues. In certain cases public funding may cover the whole gap. Two timing points: the GBER expires on 31 December 2026 and is under revision, with the revised instrument expected to absorb additional aid categories. Schemes designed on current Article 56b parameters should be reviewed against the revised text, and grant agreements should anticipate the transition.

CEEAG, IPCEI and CISAF. The Climate, Energy and Environmental Aid Guidelines of January 2022 (“CEEAG”) provide the assessment framework for notified measures outside the GBER, including aid for industrial decarbonisation within port areas and for the conversion of fossil fuel facilities. For large cross-border hydrogen and ammonia projects of the kind under development at Rotterdam, Wilhelmshaven and several Spanish ports, the Important Projects of Common European Interest framework permits aid substantially exceeding GBER thresholds, including up to the whole funding gap, where the project serves a strategic EU objective and involves genuine cross-border collaboration; the Hy2Use and Hy2Infra waves have already approved substantial funding at port locations.

The Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework (“TCTF”) expired at the end of 2025 and has been succeeded by the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (“CISAF”), adopted on 25 June 2025 and in force until 31 December 2030. CISAF makes permanent much of the relaxed approach developed under the TCTF, with simplified compatibility criteria for aid accelerating clean energy deployment, supporting industrial decarbonisation, securing clean technology manufacturing capacity and de-risking private investment; where a scheme meets the specified conditions the Commission will not analyse competitive distortion further, save for larger individual amounts. The first clearance, in August 2025, was an €11 billion French offshore wind scheme using competitive tender and two-way contracts for difference.

The move from a crisis instrument to a five-year framework matters practically: where the TCTF required renewal and carried political risk, CISAF gives Member States a stable basis for multi-year programmes without the authorising framework lapsing before the aided investment completes. It is particularly significant where transition away from fossil throughput requires industrial reconversion and retraining.

CISAF was amended on 29 April 2026 by the Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework, introducing temporary flexibility and higher intensities under the energy-intensive industry provisions to reflect the Gulf price shock, applying from March to December 2026. Ports with energy-intensive tenants should consider whether the amended provisions assist those tenants, since tenant viability is frequently the load-bearing element of the port’s own case.

In practice. The Commission’s clearances for the transformation of French ports for floating wind manufacturing show these instruments operating together. The €260 million committed through France 2030 to five strategic ports, discussed at Section 9.2, required clearance for each facility. The Commission assessed the measures under the GBER environmental and energy exemptions and, above the thresholds, under CEEAG, finding in each case a genuine market failure — the inability of private capital to finance the non-revenue-generating elements of port transformation, including dredging, reclamation, quay wall reinforcement and heavy-lift infrastructure — with aid limited to the minimum necessary to bridge the gap. The decisions confirm that the Commission treats port-based clean energy manufacturing as a legitimate aid category and provide a precedent for other Member States.

The cumulative effect is a dense landscape in which a port may access support through several channels at once, but in which cumulation rules, notification thresholds and the prohibition on overcompensation demand careful structuring.

5.4Blended finance, the Hydrogen Bank and CfDs

The Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (“STIP”) coordinates EU public resources for sustainable fuel projects and green port infrastructure. Its operating principle is blending. The EU does not fund the whole of a project; it deploys grants, concessional loans, revenue guarantees and partnership structures to absorb the highest-risk elements of the capital stack, reducing the residual risk to a level at which commercial lenders, including the EIB, will provide the balance. Where a port proposes a €100 million OPS network, a €30 million grant covering the riskiest phase can render the residual €70 million financeable, because the grant has absorbed the technology and demand risk that would otherwise deter private capital. The same funding gap methodology underpins the GBER and CEEAG analysis above; the two operate as one system. Access is governed by the dual filter described at Section 5.2.

The European Hydrogen Bank. The Bank operates a competitive reverse auction. Producers bid the minimum subsidy per kilogram at which they can produce competitively, and the Commission awards fixed premium contracts — up to €4.50 per kilogram for up to ten years — to the most cost-efficient, bridging the green premium while imposing competitive discipline on subsidy allocation.

The RFNBO delegated acts. Eligibility for that support, and the compliance value of the output under FuelEU, both depend on whether the hydrogen qualifies as a renewable fuel of non-biological origin under RED III. That is governed by Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2023/1184 and 2023/1185, and it is the single most important technical constraint on port-based electrolysis. Grid-connected electrolysers must satisfy three tests.

Additionality requires the renewable electricity to derive from installations commissioned no earlier than 36 months before the electrolyser and not in receipt of operating aid, save in specified cases. Temporal correlation requires generation and electrolysis to be matched monthly until the end of 2029 and hourly from 1 January 2030. Geographic correlation requires both to sit in the same bidding zone, or in an interconnected zone with equal or higher prices.

The interaction with the microgrid strategy at Section 2.1 is direct, and favourable. An electrolyser supplied by direct line from a renewable installation, without recourse to the public grid, is treated more permissively than a grid-connected one — so the structure ports are adopting to circumvent connection queues may also be the structure that secures RFNBO status for the hydrogen produced.

Conversely, a port running an electrolyser on grid electricity supported by power purchase agreements must construct those agreements to satisfy all three tests and plan for hourly matching from 2030. Where the output is destined for bunkering, the RFNBO determination also drives the multiplier and sub-quota treatment at Section 3.1, and the two analyses should be conducted together.

Contracts for difference. The CfD has become the EU’s default instrument for long-term revenue certainty. A public authority guarantees a price per unit of output, topping up where the market price falls below the strike price and recovering the surplus where it exceeds it. The 2024 electricity market design rules require Member States to use CfDs or equivalent two-way premiums for new publicly supported renewable capacity, and the Hydrogen Bank’s fixed premium contracts operate in substance as one-way CfDs.

The consequence for port infrastructure is indirect but substantial. Where a port-based electrolyser, e-fuel facility or ammonia plant benefits from a CfD, the guaranteed revenue is a bankable long-duration cash flow assignable to project finance lenders, and the quayside reinforcement, connection, pipeline and storage assets serving it benefit indirectly, because the throughput or capacity payments on which their own revenue model depends are underwritten by the price guarantee. A grant absorbing construction and technology risk at the front end, combined with a CfD securing revenue risk across the operating life, confines residual lender risk to a band of operational performance risk within conventional project finance tolerances. Section 9.4 describes the clearest working example.

Instrument stacking. At Rotterdam, CEF grants have financed high-voltage connections and sub-sea cable infrastructure; EIB loans have funded electrolyser capacity and automated electric cargo-handling equipment; and Innovation Fund awards have supported the Porthos carbon capture project, transporting captured CO2 from industrial emitters in the port area to depleted North Sea gas fields. No single public fund bears the whole project risk, while the aggregate contribution renders the programme bankable for private co-investors. The approach is becoming the standard model for large-scale port decarbonisation.

5.5Revenue diversification: the commercial case for the decarbonised port

The preceding subsections concern how capital cost is financed. Equally significant, and frequently underappreciated, is the extent to which a decarbonised port earns revenue from services that did not exist under the conventional model. Five channels are material.

Metered utility supply. OPS turns the port from a provider of berthing space into a supplier of a metered utility, charging per kilowatt-hour at a tariff recovering connection capital cost, electricity cost and a margin. For ports with substantial call volumes the aggregate is significant, recurring and contractually secured through mandatory connection obligations. Ports generating behind the meter capture the full margin between self-generation cost and tariff rather than passing most of it to a supplier — an advantage that widens where wholesale prices are volatile or connection charges high, as they have been across 2026. The channel rests on a legal premise rarely stated: the port must be entitled to sell electricity to third parties, which is determined by the closed distribution system and licensing analysis at Section 2.1. A port that has invested in generation without resolving that question may be able to reduce its own costs but not to monetise the surplus.

Participation in the fuel value chain. Under the landlord model, fuel-related revenue was confined to land rents from third-party storage operators and modest throughput fees. The decarbonised port may participate directly, through equity in production joint ventures, revenue-sharing with producers and suppliers, or operation of port-owned storage and distribution on a tolling basis.

That is a different commercial posture with different regulatory consequences, including those at Section 10.4.

Novel commodity throughput. Handling hydrogen, ammonia, liquefied CO2 and synthetic fuels as import, export or transhipment cargo generates throughput fees, storage charges and handling revenues additional to the conventional base.

Rotterdam’s role in Porthos and Aramis illustrates the scale: throughput and storage revenues from CO2 captured across north-western Europe, a commodity flow that did not exist five years ago and that grows as the ETS price rises. Where the port secures long-term capacity reservation or take-or-pay commitments of the type negotiated through open-season processes at Rotterdam and Antwerp, the revenues are transformative rather than incremental.

Premium industrial tenancy. Clean energy manufacturing generates land rents substantially above those from cargo storage, reflecting specialised infrastructure, scarcity of alternative sites and the ten to twenty year duration of exclusive commitment contracts. The advantage is compounded by ancillary activity: component supply chains, workforce services, marine logistics and maintenance.

Northern European ports that have repositioned legacy oil and gas infrastructure for fixed offshore wind already demonstrate

this, with operations and maintenance contracts providing recurring income across the twenty-five to thirty year life of the installations they serve.

Environmental differentiation of charges. A growing number of ports offer reduced dues to vessels demonstrating superior environmental performance while imposing surcharges or withholding priority berthing from those that do not. Gothenburg operates a discount programme linked to the Clean Shipping Index and the Environmental Ship Index; Antwerp-Bruges applies differentiated dues rewarding vessels using LNG, methanolnor shore power and extends preferential berth allocation to harbour craft on high-blend biofuels. The mechanism generates a higher effective tariff net of discounts than a flat structure and attracts a clientele whose presence enhances the port’s standing with cargo owners subject to their own reporting obligations.

Its legal basis and constraints come from the Port Services Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/352), more often mentioned as an instrument under review than applied as operative law. Port infrastructure charges must be transparent, objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate, and may be differentiated according to commercial practice or in pursuit of improved environmental performance provided the criteria are relevant, objective and publicly available. A structure that cannot be justified against those criteria is exposed to challenge, the more so where the port authority is dominant. The Regulation is also the source of the rules on market access for port services including bunkering, and of the grounds on which an authority may limit the number of providers — a question that becomes acute as ports move to license a smaller number of technically capable methanol and ammonia suppliers, as Section 8 describes.

Together these channels change the financial profile of the port.

A port that has invested across the range holds a diversified portfolio that improves revenue resilience, reduces exposure to cyclical cargo volumes and improves the bankability of future investment. For slower ports the gap is structural rather than merely competitive: as requirements tighten, operators will concentrate calls where the full suite of infrastructure exists, and ports unable to provide it face progressive erosion of commercial relevance alongside regulatory non-compliance.

5.6Energy taxation

Two fiscal features distort every comparison between conventional and alternative marine fuels, and both are routinely omitted from project appraisals.

Marine bunker fuel supplied for navigation in EU waters, other than for private pleasure craft, benefits from a mandatory excise exemption under the Energy Taxation Directive. Conventional bunkers are untaxed, so the price differential against alternative fuels understates the underlying cost differential seen in every other transport mode and overstates the incremental burden carbon pricing imposes.

The proposed recast would narrow the exemption but remains blocked in Council, where it requires unanimity.

Electricity supplied to vessels at berth is treated differently. Member States have obtained Council authorisations permitting reduced rates on shore-side electricity, and the availability and level of that relief is a direct input into the OPS tariff and therefore into the revenue analysis above. Where a relief is time-limited, its expiry should be checked against the tenor of any related financing.

6.Progress and specialisation across European ports

Progress is markedly uneven, reflecting disparities in financial capacity, geography, national policy and legacy infrastructure. Drawing on ESPO, IAPH WorldmPorts Sustainability Program and other industry data, three categories may be observed, and within them a clear pattern of specialisation.

The trailblazers. Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg lead, benefiting from deep institutional capacity, diversified revenue, strong national support and established relationships with global lines and energy majors. Rotterdam is the pre-eminent European hub for the energy transition, with Porthos and Aramis, a hydrogen backbone, e-fuel capacity and substantial behind-the-meter generation. Antwerp-Bruges leverages Europe’s largest integrated chemical cluster to anchor demand for hydrogen and sustainable feedstocks. Hamburg is investing in OPS and automated terminals, and in the hydrogen import terminal at neighbouring Wilhelmshaven, where a large-scale ammonia cracking facility is under development.

The fast movers. Algeciras, Bilbao and Barcelona in Spain, Marseille, Gothenburg and Piraeus are advancing rapidly, in several cases ahead of regulatory deadlines, supported by proactive national strategies, favourable geography and targeted investment in niche capability.

The catch-up category. Many smaller regional and bulk facilities, particularly in southern and eastern Europe, remain at an early stage. While ESPO data indicates approximately 78% of European ports now have formal environmental targets, translation into infrastructure lags: industry surveys suggest only 11% to 19% of major commercial berths have operational OPS, and around 8% of ports have hydrogen refuelling in place or under construction. The barriers are principally financial — capital costs disproportionate to the revenue base, and EU funding that remains competitive and administratively complex. The capacity-building programme announced with the Ports Strategy and delivered with EIB Advisory targets precisely this constraint.

Specialisation. Rather than serving every segment, leading ports concentrate where they hold comparative advantage. In e-fuels and bio-LNG, Bilbao is developing a €146 million facility with a 10 MW electrolyser and CO2 capture, and Barcelona has become the leading Mediterranean hub for bio-LNG and renewable methanol bunkering under long-term supply agreements. In ammonia and hydrogen, Algeciras is building dedicated storage and deploying a 7,500 cubic metre ammonia bunker vessel to serve traffic transiting the Strait of Gibraltar, while Wilhelmshaven develops as Germany’s principal ammonia import and cracking hub. In carbon capture, Rotterdam leads with Porthos and Aramis, supported by emerging CO2 export clusters in the Baltic and south-eastern Europe.

7.Spain’s renewable energy advantage

Spain’s solar irradiance and onshore wind resources enable renewable electricity at a levelised cost significantly below northern Europe. The advantage translates directly into cheaper green hydrogen, electrolysis being highly energy-intensive, and by extension into lower-cost e-fuels and ammonia.

Spanish ports are exploiting this both to position themselves as production and export hubs and to build on-site generation that bypasses the grid constraints afflicting ports elsewhere. Bilbao, anticipating a sixfold increase in local demand by 2030, is deploying approximately 50 MW across its docks and a dedicated port-side wind installation. Valencia has taken the different route described at Section 2.4.

The cost advantage is amplified by the geographic correlation requirement in the RFNBO delegated acts, which favours co-location of electrolysis with low-cost generation in the same bidding zone — a test on which Spain’s position is unusually strong. These initiatives are transforming the Iberian Peninsula from a peripheral energy island into a central node of the European clean energy supply chain, and establishing a model of port-level energy self-sufficiency being studied closely elsewhere.

8.Sustainable marine fuel bunkering

Bunkering was historically a straightforward operation: heavy fuel oil or marine gas oil pumped from a shore tank or barge through standardised manifold connections, with minimal regulatory complexity beyond safety and quantity verification.

FuelEU Maritime and AFIR, with the tightening of IMO limits, have produced a structural shift in which ports must accommodate biofuel blends, green methanol, ammonia, bio-LNG and synthetic e-fuels, each with distinct challenges of chemical stability, toxicity, flammability, segregation, delivery engineering and documentation. Bunkering has become a technical, risk-managed operation with significant implications for infrastructure investment, terminal design, safety regulation and risk allocation.

8.1Physical storage and delivery infrastructure

Handling has diverged into two pathways.

The first concerns drop-in biofuels, which blend with conventional distillates and combust in existing engines without modification. Their compatibility makes them attractive, but their storage characteristics introduce complications conventional terminals were not designed for. Chief among these is microbial degradation: unlike stable petroleum products, biofuels are hygroscopic and absorb moisture from the marine atmosphere, creating conditions for rapid bacterial and fungal proliferation in storage tanks. The resulting sludge can block filters, foul injectors and in severe cases render a consignment unusable, with serious consequences for propulsion safety mid-voyage. This imposes strict limits on storage duration and requires enhanced tank monitoring, water drainage and biocide protocols.

Equally consequential is the requirement for complete physical segregation of fuel types and blending ratios. To prevent cross-contamination, which can destabilise fuel properties and invalidate the sustainability certifications on which compliance depends, terminals must maintain separate tank farms, piping, manifold connections and in many cases dedicated barges for each specification.

This substantially increases capital cost and spatial footprint and is driving a redesign of terminal layouts at multi-fuel hubs.

The second pathway concerns fuels chemically incompatible with conventional infrastructure. Green methanol, though liquid at ambient conditions, has a much lower flashpoint than marine diesel and presents a substantial fire and explosion risk during transfer; ports are deploying closed-loop vapour recovery and inerted piping with enhanced fire suppression. Ammonia is more demanding still: acutely toxic at low concentrations and lethal to marine organisms, it requires automated emergency breakaway couplings, continuous leak detection capable of triggering instantaneous pump shutdown, and comprehensive exclusion zones.

Both engage the full rigour of Seveso III, requiring safety reports, emergency plans and in many jurisdictions hazardous substances consents, all adding materially to cost and lead time.

8.2Contractual adaptation

BIMCO has responded with standardised clauses, including the Biofuel Clause for Time Charter Parties and the FuelEU Maritime Clause, allocating novel operational, financial and regulatory risk between owners, time and voyage charterers and suppliers.

Speed and consumption warranties. Because alternative fuels contain less energy per unit volume than heavy fuel oil, a vessel must consume a greater volume for the same propulsive output, so traditional speed-and-consumption warranties no longer hold. The Biofuel Clause requires the parties to recalibrate them whenever alternative fuels are introduced, and establishes a mandatory testing protocol under which the charterer must procure independent laboratory analysis at its own cost and at a jointly appointed facility before the owner must accept the fuel. This protects the owner against engine damage from off-specification blends and provides an evidentiary basis for disputes.

The documentation chain. FuelEU requires owners to prove with documentary precision the lifecycle carbon intensity of every unit consumed. Assertion is insufficient: verified data must be submitted to the regulatory database, supported by Bunker Delivery Notes and accompanying Sustainability Proof or Proof of Compliance certificates issued by the supplier and authenticated under the applicable framework. The FuelEU Maritime Clause obliges charterer and supplier to furnish the master with a compliant note and certification at delivery, and provides that where documentation is absent, inaccurate or incomplete the charterer bears immediate liability for penalties, compliance deficits and additional ETS costs. The allocation reflects the reality that the owner, while bearing the reporting obligation, depends wholly on upstream counterparties for the provenance information.

Storage life and redelivery. Biofuels degrade and cannot remain in a vessel’s tanks indefinitely without falling below specification. Modern clauses stipulate maximum storage duration on board, requiring the charterer either to ensure consumption within the period or to bear the cost of pumping degraded fuel ashore. A related issue concerns valuation of remaining bunkers on redelivery: under standard terms the charterer is credited at conventional fuel rates, substantially below the premium paid for certified sustainable fuels. The updated Biofuel Clause allows the parties to pre-agree a separate premium pricing scale, so that charterers are not penalised at redelivery. Negotiation of these provisions is now a material commercial issue on longer time charters.

For ports the cumulative effect is a new layer of governance complexity. Attracting calls requires investment not only in multi-fuel storage and delivery but in the digital systems, laboratory capability and documentation platforms supporting the chain of custody. Licensing bunker suppliers, historically routine, becomes substantive: the authority must satisfy itself that licensees have the technical capability, safety management systems and certification infrastructure to handle fuels with materially different hazard profiles. Where that leads to restricting the number of suppliers, the Port Services Regulation constraints at Section 5.5 apply.

8.3Ammonia as a marine fuel: the code gap and the liability gap

Section 13 addresses ammonia carried as cargo. Ammonia used as fuel raises separate and, for port authorities, more immediate questions.

There is no chapter of the IMO’s IGF Code governing ammonia. Ammonia-fuelled ships are approved through the alternative design route under SOLAS, supported by IMO interim guidelines and classification society rules, case by case and founded on risk assessment rather than prescriptive requirement. For a port authority deciding whether to permit ammonia bunkering at a berth, there is no settled international baseline against which to assess a proposed operation, and the port is in practice making its own safety determination with the assistance of the class society and the national authority. Ports developing the capability are responding with simultaneous operations studies, quantitative risk assessment, defined exclusion zones and bunkering-specific approvals in port regulations — but the underlying position is that the port carries a residual judgement a prescriptive code would otherwise carry for it.
